title: How PTSD Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder), tracing its history from "soldier's heart" in the Civil War (Jacob Mendes Da Costa) through "shell shock" in World War One (Charles Myers) to the modern diagnosis around 1980. They cover the four symptom clusters (re-experiencing, avoidance, numbing, hyperarousal), acute, chronic and delayed-onset types, child presentation, risk and protective factors (prior trauma, glucocorticoids, cortisol, personality/optimism, education, sex differences, serotonin transporter gene, epigenetics, social support), mild traumatic brain injury in the Iraq War, and treatments (cognitive processing therapy, exposure therapy, SSRIs such as Zoloft and Paxil, D-cycloserine, beta blockers, propranolol, hydrocortisone, stellate ganglion block, transcranial magnetic stimulation, Army resilience training). Credits Will Sovey for updating the article. Ends with listener mail about a Dungeons and Dragons story and sign-off.

segments.title: Introduction and thanks to Will Sovey
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, thank clinician Will Sovey for annotating and updating the outdated PTSD article, and note that June is PTSD Awareness Month.
topics: stuff you should know PTSD episode

segments.title: History: soldier's heart, shell shock, and modern PTSD
segments.summary: Early names for PTSD: Da Costa's soldier's heart after the Civil War, Charles Myers' shell shock in World War One (linked to mild traumatic brain injury), and the modern diagnosis around 1980 after Vietnam-era studies.

segments.title: What counts as trauma and PTSD diagnosis criteria
segments.summary: PTSD is a set of symptoms following trauma, which can be direct or indirect. Diagnosis requires symptoms lasting a certain period, with re-experiencing as the cornerstone. Excessive retrieval, nightmares and flashbacks are described.

segments.title: The four symptom clusters
segments.summary: The four symptom clusters are re-experiencing, avoidance, numbing with alcohol and drug use, and hyperarousal such as jumpiness, insomnia and constant guard. The hosts note the health toll of prolonged stress.

segments.title: Acute, chronic, and delayed-onset PTSD; PTSD in children
segments.summary: Acute PTSD lasts about three months, chronic lasts longer, and delayed onset appears at least six months after the trauma. Children can show PTSD through behavior and play.

segments.title: Risk and protective factors
segments.summary: Prior trauma, depleted glucocorticoids, personality traits like optimism and tackling problems head on, college education, and social support affect PTSD risk. Women are reported less likely than men, citing the Vietnam study figures.

segments.title: Genetics, epigenetics, and cortisol research
segments.summary: Research on the serotonin transporter gene and epigenetic changes, including a Detroit study of 100 people with PTSD showing more epigenetic changes, and a 2008 hydrocortisone study with soldiers.

segments.title: Iraq War, roadside bombs, and brain injury
segments.summary: Head injuries from IEDs in the Iraq War are discussed as a major factor, as improved treatment saves lives but leaves brain changes. Guerrilla warfare is described as a PTSD risk.

segments.title: PTSD treatments: therapy, medication, and experimental approaches
segments.summary: Cognitive processing therapy, exposure therapy, SSRIs Zoloft and Paxil (the only FDA-approved PTSD drugs), D-cycloserine, beta blockers, stellate ganglion block, MDMA, and transcranial magnetic stimulation are discussed, along with the Army's resilience training and historical Iroquois post-war practices.

segments.title: Listener mail: D&D story from Christina
segments.summary: Listener Christina from Cleveland shares a story of her parents' and uncles' 1980s Dungeons and Dragons sessions recorded on tape. Hosts respond and give contact info.
